title: The Three DMA Modes: Burst, Cycle Stealing, Transparent
quickIdea: The modes differ in how the bus is shared. Burst takes it for the whole block, cycle stealing takes one cycle at a time, and transparent takes only cycles the CPU was not using anyway.
remember: Burst (block) mode: the controller keeps the bus until the whole block is moved. Highest throughput, and the CPU is stalled for the duration.
Cycle stealing: the controller takes one bus cycle, transfers one word, and releases the bus, repeating at intervals. The CPU is slowed by the fraction of cycles stolen, not stopped.
Transparent mode: the controller uses only cycles in which the CPU is not using the bus. No slowdown at all, but the transfer may take arbitrarily long and can starve.

Cycle stealing is the mode that makes DMA compatible with a CPU that must keep running; burst is the mode that maximises throughput - which is why 2024 Set 1 Q.15's claim that burst has higher throughput is true.
The choice is a straight trade: throughput against how much CPU time the transfer is allowed to take away.

example.prompt: A controller can move 8 bytes per bus cycle. It is allowed 1% of the cycles of a 4 MHz processor. What is the transfer rate in cycle stealing mode?
example.work: Stolen cycles per second = 4,000,000 x 0.01 = 40,000. Each carries 8 bytes = 64 bits. Rate = 40,000 x 64 = 2,560,000 bits per second.
example.answer: 2,560,000 bits per second, that is 25,60,000 - option (C) of GATE CSE 2024 Set 2 Q.11.

gateAngle: The modes appear as statement questions (2024 Set 1 Q.15) and as a throughput calculation (2024 Set 2 Q.11, 2021 Set 2 Q.20). The one-mark form is always the same trade stated in words: which mode blocks the CPU least, which moves data fastest, and whether one word or a block moves per stolen cycle.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2024 Set 1 Q.15: which statement is false - one word per stolen cycle, burst has higher throughput than cycle stealing, programmed I/O has better CPU utilisation than interrupt-driven I/O, or vectored interrupts start the routine faster?
variations.answer: The third: programmed I/O does not have better CPU utilisation; its busy waiting is the worst of the three.
variations.why: The other three are the standard statements of the three modes and of vectored interrupts.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2022 Q.17: which mechanism gives the highest throughput for bulk data from a hard disk to memory?
variations.why: The CPU leaves the data path entirely, so the block moves at bus speed rather than at the speed of a service routine.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: A system must never stall the CPU for more than one cycle at a time. Which mode is admissible, and what does it cost?
variations.answer: Cycle stealing: one stolen cycle at a time, so the CPU is slowed by the stolen fraction but never stopped. The cost is throughput - the block takes longer than in burst mode, and the device may overrun if it cannot wait.
variations.why: It is the reason interactive machines use cycle stealing while disk controllers often use burst.

trap.what: Believing cycle stealing stops the CPU for the whole transfer, or that transparent mode is always the best choice.
trap.why: Cycle stealing interrupts the CPU one cycle at a time, so the CPU keeps running, only slower. Transparent mode never slows the CPU but can starve the device, so it is unsuitable for a device with a deadline.
trap.counterexample: Move 1 MB in transparent mode on a machine that is 100% busy: the controller gets no cycle at all and the transfer never completes, while the CPU is at full speed. That is the worst possible outcome for the device.

check.question: Which mode gives the highest throughput, which gives the least disturbance to the CPU, and which is in between?
check.answer: Burst gives the highest throughput, transparent the least disturbance, and cycle stealing sits between them.
check.explanation: Throughput and CPU disturbance pull in opposite directions, and the three modes are the three points on that line.

visual.title: I/O Interface: Interrupt and DMA
covers: programmed I/O keeps the CPU in the status loop for the whole transfer
interrupt-driven I/O removes the wait and keeps the per-byte service routine
DMA removes the per-byte work, with cycle stealing and burst as the two sharing modes
